questions.q: What does the Information Coefficient (IC) measure?
options: The total return of a strategy
The correlation between a signal's value and the forward return it's trying to predict
The number of instruments in a universe
The volatility of a signal over time
questions.explain: IC is the correlation between a signal measured at time t and the realized forward return, averaged across dates — a direct measure of how predictive the signal actually is.

questions.q: Why can combining two genuinely predictive but lowly-correlated signals improve an information ratio?
options: Because it doubles the total position size automatically
Because averaging signals whose idiosyncratic errors aren't perfectly correlated cancels out some noise while keeping the shared real signal
Because any combination of signals is mathematically guaranteed to outperform a single signal
Because it removes the need for normalization
questions.explain: This mirrors portfolio diversification logic: if errors aren't perfectly correlated, blending reduces noise relative to the shared, real information content, which can raise the overall information ratio.

questions.q: What is the main problem with adding two signals together at equal weight when they are 0.9 correlated with each other?
options: There is no problem — equal weighting is always correct
It effectively double-counts the same underlying driver rather than adding two independent sources of information
It makes the combined signal impossible to compute
It violates data licensing agreements
questions.explain: Highly correlated signals aren't independent votes; adding them at equal weight overweights whatever shared driver they both capture rather than genuinely diversifying the combination.

questions.q: In IC-weighted combination, how is each signal's weight typically determined?
options: Randomly assigned
Equal regardless of signal quality
Proportional to the signal's own measured information coefficient relative to the others
Based solely on how recently the signal was created
questions.explain: IC weighting assigns higher weight to signals with stronger measured predictive power (higher absolute IC), so a stronger signal contributes more to the blend than a weaker one.

questions.q: What honest caveat does this lesson raise about estimating combination weights (such as IC weights) from historical data?
options: There is no caveat — estimated weights are always safe to use
Estimating weights from the same sample used to judge performance is itself a form of parameter fitting that carries overfitting risk, and should be validated out of sample
IC weighting is illegal in most jurisdictions
Weights should always be estimated using only the most recent day of data
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly compares fitting combination weights to fitting any other backtest parameter — it's subject to the same overfitting risk discussed in Chapter 4, and should be checked out-of-sample rather than trusted blindly.
